Androscoggin County.absent_or_rare: moose, black bears, and white-tailed deer live in the surrounding region but are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Androscoggin County.habitat_type: the dense mill-era housing of Lewiston and Auburn, surrounding commuter suburbs, and farmland and lake towns to the north and west
Androscoggin County.nearest_metro: Lewiston-Auburn is the county's own metro center, with Portland about 35 miles south
Androscoggin County.region: south-central Maine along the Androscoggin River, built around the Lewiston-Auburn twin cities
Androscoggin County.regional_wildlife: Norway rats are persistent in Lewiston's older triple-decker and mill-worker neighborhoods, bat colonies recur in the twin cities' older housing stock, and raccoons and skunks generate steady call volume across the Auburn, Lisbon, and Poland suburbs, with beavers flooding culverts and camp roads on the county's ponds and streams

Aroostook County.absent_or_rare: opossums are rare to absent this far north because severe winters and frostbite limit them, Canada lynx in the northern forest are federally threatened, and moose, black bears, and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Aroostook County.habitat_type: open potato farmland across the south and center, small service towns along US-1, and vast commercial forest in the north and west
Aroostook County.nearest_metro: Bangor (about 115 miles south of Houlton), with Edmundston, New Brunswick just across the border from Madawaska
Aroostook County.region: northern Maine along the Canadian border, the largest county by land area in the state
Aroostook County.regional_wildlife: porcupines gnaw sheds, camp siding, and vehicle lines throughout the North Woods towns, groundhogs burrow along the edges of potato fields and farmyards, and beavers flood woods roads and culverts across the county, while bat colonies in older farmhouses around Presque Isle, Caribou, and Houlton are a recurring summer issue

Cumberland County.absent_or_rare: moose are uncommon in this developed coastal county, and black bears and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Cumberland County.habitat_type: the urban Portland core, dense suburbs around Casco Bay, and the Sebago Lake camp and cottage country inland
Cumberland County.nearest_metro: Portland is itself the state's largest metro center
Cumberland County.region: southern Maine on Casco Bay, the most populous county in the state and home to Portland
Cumberland County.regional_wildlife: Norway rats are persistent around Portland's older housing and working waterfront, opossums are well established in the mild coastal suburbs, raccoons and skunks generate heavy call volume in Scarborough, Gorham, and Falmouth, and bat colonies in older Portland and Westbrook homes plus seasonal camps on Sebago Lake are recurring summer issues

Franklin County.absent_or_rare: opossums are scarce at this elevation and latitude, and moose, black bears, and white-tailed deer — all common in the Rangeley region — are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Franklin County.habitat_type: the Farmington college-town valley and southern farmland, rising to ski, lake, and sporting-camp country around Rangeley and Carrabassett Valley
Franklin County.region: western Maine foothills and mountains, from the Farmington valley to the Rangeley lakes
Franklin County.regional_wildlife: porcupines damage camps, outhouses, and outbuildings around Rangeley Lake and the western lakes, bat colonies are a recurring issue in seasonal camps that sit closed all winter, and beavers flood camp roads and low ground along the Sandy River and its tributaries, with fishers causing occasional chicken-coop losses on rural homesteads

Hancock County.absent_or_rare: opossums are still uncommon away from the immediate coast, and moose, black bears, and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Hancock County.habitat_type: Acadia and Mount Desert Island seasonal homes, working fishing villages along the peninsulas, and blueberry barrens and forest inland
Hancock County.region: coastal Maine between Penobscot Bay and Frenchman Bay, including Mount Desert Island and Acadia
Hancock County.regional_wildlife: raccoons move into Bar Harbor and Mount Desert seasonal homes that sit empty in the off-season, porcupines gnaw camp and outbuilding woodwork around the inland ponds, bat colonies recur in older Ellsworth and island houses, and beavers flood low roads and driveways along the Union River tributaries

Kennebec County.absent_or_rare: moose, black bears, and white-tailed deer live in the surrounding region but are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Kennebec County.habitat_type: the Augusta and Waterville urban cores, river-valley suburbs, and a ring of lake-camp communities and farmland
Kennebec County.nearest_metro: Augusta is the county's own regional center, with Portland about 55 miles southwest
Kennebec County.region: central Maine along the Kennebec River valley, including the state capital at Augusta
Kennebec County.regional_wildlife: Norway rats and raccoons are steady in older Augusta and Waterville neighborhoods, bat colonies recur in the valley's older housing and in lake camps on Cobbosseecontee and Messalonskee lakes, and groundhogs and skunks are routine garden and under-deck problems across the Winthrop, Oakland, and Gardiner suburbs

Knox County.absent_or_rare: moose are uncommon on the coastal peninsulas, and black bears and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Knox County.habitat_type: harbor towns and seasonal homes along the peninsulas, the island communities of Vinalhaven and North Haven, and wooded inland towns
Knox County.nearest_metro: Portland (about 80 miles southwest of Rockland) and Bangor (about 65 miles northeast)
Knox County.region: midcoast Maine on the western shore of Penobscot Bay, a county of peninsulas and island towns
Knox County.regional_wildlife: raccoons and bats are recurring problems in Camden, Rockport, and Thomaston seasonal homes closed up for winter, Norway rats persist around Rockland's working waterfront, and porcupines damage outbuildings and camps in the wooded inland towns of Warren, Union, and Appleton

Lincoln County.absent_or_rare: moose are rare on the midcoast peninsulas, and black bears and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Lincoln County.habitat_type: tidal river towns, fishing villages at the ends of the peninsulas, and a high share of seasonal coastal homes
Lincoln County.nearest_metro: Portland (about 50 miles southwest of Wiscasset), with Bath and Brunswick about 15 miles west
Lincoln County.region: midcoast Maine between the Kennebec and Damariscotta rivers, a county of long tidal peninsulas
Lincoln County.regional_wildlife: raccoons and bats move into Boothbay Harbor, Bristol, and South Bristol cottages during the long off-season, opossums are established along this mild stretch of coast, and porcupines and beavers cause steady camp and culvert problems in the wooded interior towns of Waldoboro, Whitefield, and Jefferson

Oxford County.absent_or_rare: opossums are scarce in the colder western mountains, and moose, black bears, and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Oxford County.habitat_type: the Rumford mill town and eastern farm towns, ski and second-home country around Bethel, and lake camps across the western mountains
Oxford County.nearest_metro: Lewiston-Auburn (about 30 miles east of Paris), with Portland about 45 miles southeast
Oxford County.region: western Maine along the New Hampshire border, from farmland in the east to White Mountain foothills in the west
Oxford County.regional_wildlife: porcupines and beavers are the steady camp-country nuisances around Bethel, Fryeburg, and the western lakes, bat colonies recur in older Rumford and Norway housing and in seasonal camps, and fishers cause occasional chicken-coop and outbuilding losses on farms in the Oxford Hills

Penobscot County.absent_or_rare: Canada lynx in the northern forest are federally threatened, and moose, black bears, and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Penobscot County.habitat_type: the Bangor-Brewer urban core and suburbs, university neighborhoods in Orono, mill towns upriver, and extensive forest in the north
Penobscot County.nearest_metro: Bangor is itself the regional metro center for northern and eastern Maine
Penobscot County.region: central Maine along the Penobscot River, built around Bangor and running north into working forest
Penobscot County.regional_wildlife: Norway rats and raccoons are persistent in Bangor's older neighborhoods, university-area housing in Orono draws raccoon and skunk pressure, bat colonies recur in older homes across Bangor, Brewer, and Old Town, and beavers and porcupines are routine problems at camps and rural properties upriver toward Millinocket

Piscataquis County.absent_or_rare: opossums are essentially absent and Norway rats are confined to the few larger towns, Canada lynx are federally threatened, and moose, black bears, and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Piscataquis County.habitat_type: vast commercial and conservation forest, lake camps and sporting camps, and a handful of small service towns
Piscataquis County.region: the Maine Highlands in north-central Maine, the state's least populous county, built around Moosehead Lake and Baxter State Park
Piscataquis County.regional_wildlife: porcupines gnaw camp siding, outhouses, and equipment around Moosehead Lake and the interior ponds, beavers flood camp roads and tote roads across the county, and bat colonies in lake camps and older Dover-Foxcroft and Greenville homes are discovered when camps are opened in spring, with red squirrels a constant camp and attic problem

Sagadahoc County.absent_or_rare: moose are rare in this small, developed coastal county, and black bears and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Sagadahoc County.habitat_type: the Bath shipbuilding town, fast-growing Topsham suburbs, and quiet coastal peninsulas in Phippsburg and Georgetown
Sagadahoc County.nearest_metro: Portland (about 30 miles southwest of Bath), with Brunswick immediately west in Cumberland County
Sagadahoc County.region: the lower Kennebec River and Merrymeeting Bay coast, the smallest county in Maine by land area
Sagadahoc County.regional_wildlife: raccoons, skunks, and opossums are steady across the Topsham and West Bath suburbs, bat colonies recur in Bath's older housing near the shipyard, moles damage lawns in the county's suburban neighborhoods, and raccoons move into Phippsburg and Georgetown seasonal cottages over the winter

Somerset County.absent_or_rare: opossums are scarce north of the southern farm towns, Canada lynx in the northern forest are federally threatened, and moose, black bears, and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Somerset County.habitat_type: mill and farm towns along the Kennebec in the south, and logging forest, sporting camps, and the Moose River valley in the north
Somerset County.nearest_metro: Waterville and Augusta (about 35 to 40 miles south of Skowhegan)
Somerset County.region: central and northwestern Maine along the upper Kennebec River, running from farm towns to the Canadian border at Jackman
Somerset County.regional_wildlife: groundhogs and skunks are routine problems in the Skowhegan, Fairfield, and Pittsfield farm country, porcupines and beavers damage camps and flood woods roads from Bingham to Jackman, and bat colonies recur in older mill-town housing and in seasonal camps along Wyman Lake and the Moose River

Waldo County.absent_or_rare: moose are uncommon along the settled coast, and black bears and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Waldo County.habitat_type: the Belfast harbor town and coastal villages, backed by small farms and wooded rural towns inland
Waldo County.region: the western shore of Penobscot Bay, between the midcoast and Bangor
Waldo County.regional_wildlife: raccoons and bats are recurring problems in Belfast and Searsport homes and seasonal properties, groundhogs burrow in gardens and fields across the Unity and Monroe farm country, and porcupines and beavers cause steady outbuilding and culvert problems in the wooded inland towns

Washington County.absent_or_rare: opossums are rare this far Downeast, and moose, black bears (common around the blueberry barrens), and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
Washington County.habitat_type: fishing villages and port towns on a rugged coast, wild blueberry barrens, and extensive low-density forest inland
Washington County.nearest_metro: Bangor (about 88 miles west of Machias), with St. Stephen, New Brunswick across the river from Calais
Washington County.region: far Downeast Maine along the Canadian border, the easternmost county in the United States
Washington County.regional_wildlife: porcupines damage camps and outbuildings throughout the inland woods, beavers flood roads and blueberry land along the county's many streams, bat colonies recur in the older housing of Eastport, Lubec, and Machias, and raccoons are a steady problem around fishing-village homes and seasonal cottages on Cobscook and Passamaquoddy bays

York County.absent_or_rare: Maine has no venomous snakes — the timber rattlesnake is extirpated from the state — and the state-endangered black racer of the southern York County barrens is protected, not a removal target; moose are uncommon this far south, and black bears and white-tailed deer are managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife rather than private wildlife removal contractors
York County.habitat_type: dense beach towns mixing year-round and seasonal housing, mill-era housing in Biddeford and Sanford, and rural towns inland to the west
York County.nearest_metro: Portland (about 28 miles north of Biddeford), with Portsmouth, New Hampshire immediately across the river from Kittery
York County.region: southernmost Maine along the New Hampshire border and the York County coast, the state's second most populous county
York County.regional_wildlife: opossums are better established in York County than anywhere else in Maine thanks to its mildest winters, Norway rats persist in Biddeford and Sanford mill-era neighborhoods, raccoons work the beach rental towns from Kittery to Old Orchard Beach, and bat colonies recur in the county's old farmhouses and coastal cottages, with moles damaging lawns across the southern suburbs

state.agency: Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife
state.climate_factor: Maine's long, cold winters and heavy snow push rodents, bats, and squirrels into attics and wall voids aggressively, and the state's large stock of seasonal camps and coastal cottages sits vacant all winter, so intrusions are often discovered months after they start when buildings are opened in spring
state.name: Maine
state.peak_intrusion_season: April through May as squirrels and raccoons raise spring litters and seasonal camps are opened for the first time since fall, June and July for bat maternity colonies in attics, and late September through November as rodents, squirrels, and cluster-seeking animals move into heated buildings ahead of winter
state.permit_note: Maine does not issue a general nuisance wildlife control operator license; commercial nuisance work runs through MDIFW's Animal Damage Control (ADC) agent certification under MDIFW Chapter 27 rules, ADC agents act as agents of the Commissioner and must also hold a valid Maine trapping license, and moose, black bears, deer, and other large game fall under direct Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife management rather than the private wildlife removal industry
